cells.tense: You are at the bench, hands on the frame, adjusting as you go.
cells.ask: Add one piece before you subtract anything today. Notice what the addition tells you about the whole.
cells.core:
You're at the bench, and the work is moving. Not pushing — responding. You add a piece, the whole shifts, you feel the shift, you adjust again. That's the pattern, and it's working. What you're building came out of something that got cleared away, and you know that's why it holds. You're not forcing the frame into a shape it won't take.

The balance lives in the ongoing adjustment. Miss a day of it and the structure starts talking back. So the ask is to keep the contact: put one thing in today and read what changes. The work wants a hand on it, not a plan for it.
cells.sheetLine: You're building it by feel, and the feel is accurate.
cells.verb: raising the first working frame of something that didn't exist before
cells.place: the workbench where you keep adjusting the hinge until it swings true

cells.tense: You will have built it by the time you stop rehearsing what it should become.
cells.ask: Say the current version out loud to one person today, including the parts you'd normally fix first.
cells.core:
The thing isn't finished, and you're treating it as if it must be before anyone sees it. You keep revising ahead of the moment it's actually for — a version two steps out, a version that hasn't been tested, a version that doesn't exist yet. Meanwhile the version in front of you is starved of the contact that would finish it.

The adjusting has tipped into pre-emptive fixing. The restlessness is wearing the bench down. What loosens this is bringing a rough piece into the open early. It doesn't ask for a fix; it asks to meet a hand that isn't yours. The structure will tell you more from one real reaction than from another week of private revision.

cells.tense: You stopped at the frame and you still call it a work in progress.
cells.ask: Pick up one piece you already have and place it. Ten minutes, no plan for the rest.
cells.core:
The bench is where you left it. You know this. At some point the work called for more than the bench could give, and you stepped back from it. From there it's been easier to call it ongoing than to sit down again. The materials are still there. The skill didn't leave.

What's missing is the next physical act, however small. Not a new plan, not a better method — one placement of one piece you already chose. That is the way back in: not pushing yourself into feeling like working, but letting the work pull the feeling back. Your hands have made sense of structures before. Put them back on it and the sense returns.

cells.tense: You're already building it in every choice you make about what comes next.
cells.ask: Name one thing at the bench that exists because you decided it, not because it was inevitable.
cells.core:
You talk about the direction as if it were obvious — as if anyone would have done it this way. But look at the joins. The choices about what stays and what goes are yours. The shape it's taking is yours. You've been steering this thing from the first day, and you keep describing it as if you just found it that way.

The building is happening; the saying-so isn't. Say it out loud once, about one decision you made — not the work making itself — and the answer about who's building this comes back into your own mouth, where it belongs.
cells.sheetLine: You built this. Start saying so.
